title: Immigration (E3, full, en)
text:
The United States of America has long been the world’s chief receiving nation for immigrants. An immigrant is a person who leaves his or her country to settle and live in another country. Over the years, many millions of people have left family and friends and uprooted their lives to move to the United States. Some immigrants may feel forced to leave their homes. For example, they may fear for their lives or wellbeing due to dangers in their home countries. Their home countries may be at war. They may experience religious persecution, or not have freedom to practice their faith. Immigrants may also leave home in search of new opportunities. Whatever the reason, immigrants leave a life that is familiar for one that is unknown.

Since the United States was established in the late 1700s, there have been several waves of immigration. From about 1820 to 1870, millions of people made the voyage to the United States, mostly from northern and western Europe. The largest group of these immigrants were Irish people trying to escape a famine that plagued Ireland in the mid-1840s. Another large group from this wave were German people. Chinese people also began to immigrate to the United States during this time. They heard about opportunities to make money, like mining in California during the Gold Rush. These immigrants who arrived in the U.S. weren't always welcomed by those who had already been living there for some time. Some feared these newcomers would take away the jobs they held. Others had a hard time accepting differences, like the politics, customs, and/or religions the new immigrants brought with them. For example, many Irish people were discriminated against for being Roman Catholic. Chinese people also suffered greatly from discrimination and racism.

Another wave of U.S. immigration, roughly between 1881 and 1920, was by far the largest. During this period, most immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe. By this time, anti-immigration sentiments in the U.S. became so strong that a growing number of people demanded laws to make it harder for foreigners to become U.S. citizens. In 1875, the U.S. Congress passed its first immigration law intended to limit immigration, the Page Act. It banned certain groups of people from immigrating to the United States. One reason people supported the Page Act of 1875 was because it kept out people like convicts. At the same time, this act unfairly discriminated against some groups, like Chinese women. In 1882, Congress also passed the Chinese Exclusion Act. It prohibited Chinese workers from coming to the United States. A few years later, other laws limiting immigration were passed. One required adult immigrants to have literacy skills in a language. Another limited the number of immigrants from countries outside the Western Hemisphere. These laws caused immigration to decrease for certain groups. However, one of the greatest blows to immigration was the Great Depression of the 1930s. Immigration sharply declined. In fact, there were more people leaving the United States than coming to the country during that time.

Throughout history, immigration to the United States has continued to rise and fall due to world events and the passage of different United States laws. For example, there was a shortage of laborers during World War II, so the United States started the Bracero Program. This program allowed Mexican immigrants to come to the United States to work for a period of time. After World War II, many European immigrants fled homes ruined by war and arrived in the United States. Beginning in 1965, many immigrants moved to the United States from Asia, South America, and Mexico. A major reason for this was that the United States stopped limiting the number of immigrants it would accept from these countries. Waves of immigration to the United States continue until today.

Immigrants have come to the United States with the hope of building a better life. Many immigrants have faced discrimination by people already living in the country who feared the economic and cultural impacts of these newcomers. Despite these struggles, immigrants have contributed to the United States. They have created communities of neighbors and friends. They have introduced new food, art, and cultures to the country. And they have helped jobs and businesses grow and supported the nation’s economy. Immigrants are an important part of the fabric of the United States.
